name: Coding–Decoding — Secret Letter Codes
whatIsIt: In coding–decoding, a word is turned into a code by a hidden rule — most often 'shift each letter forward or backward by a fixed number of places'. Find the shift by comparing ONE known letter with its code, then apply the same shift to decode or encode any other word.
whyNeeded: Coding–decoding is a guaranteed scorer in reasoning papers. It is really just letter-series thinking applied to whole words, and the same shift trick cracks most questions in seconds.
realLifeUses: Foundation for how computers encode text

vocabulary.meaning: How many places each letter moves in the alphabet (+ forward, − backward).
Turn a real word into its code.
Turn a code back into the real word (shift the opposite way).
A code where every letter moves the same number of places.

story.title: One Letter Gives the Secret Away
story.text: Arjun writes: 'If CAT is coded as DBU, what is DOG?' Meera checks just one letter: C→D is +1. She tests another: A→B is +1, T→U is +1. 'The whole code is shift +1!' So DOG → E, P, H = EPH. To decode, she shifts the opposite way (−1). Meera's rule: compare one letter with its code to find the shift, then apply it everywhere.
story.answerInStory: EPH — the code is 'shift each letter +1', so D→E, O→P, G→H.

visual.caption: A '+1' code moves every letter forward one place: C→D, A→B, T→U. Find the shift from one letter, then apply it to all.

teachingGallery.title: Find the shift from one letter, then apply it
teachingGallery.note: Compare a letter with its code → that's the shift. Same shift encodes; opposite shift decodes.

examples.caption: A '+3' code (classic Caesar): A→D, B→E, C→F.

standardMethod.summary: Line up the word with its code, find the shift from one letter pair, confirm on a second, then apply the same shift (or its opposite to decode).
steps: Write the word above its code, letter by letter.
Find the shift for one pair (e.g. C→D is +1).
Confirm the shift is the same on another pair.
Apply that shift to the new word to encode, or the opposite shift to decode. Wrap around after Z.

alternateMethods.name: Use position numbers
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When the shift is large or you keep miscounting letters.
steps: Add the shift to each new letter's position, then convert back (wrap past 26).

workedExamples.problem: If DOG is coded FQI, what is the code for CAT?
steps: D→F is +2, O→Q is +2, G→I is +2 — shift is +2.

workedExamples.problem: A code shifts +1. Decode the message EPH.
steps: To decode, shift the opposite way: −1.

trickPractice.trick: Compare one letter → get the shift → apply it
trickPractice.intro: You only need ONE letter pair to unlock the whole code.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shifting forward when you should decode (shift backward), or vice-versa.
commonMistakes.fix: Encoding uses the shift as given; DECODING uses the opposite sign. If +3 made the code, decode with −3.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing the shift without checking a known letter pair.
commonMistakes.fix: Never assume. Compare at least one letter with its code to MEASURE the shift, then confirm on a second pair.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend to crack CAT=DBU → DOG=EPH. Show how comparing just C→D reveals the +1 shift, and explain that decoding uses the opposite shift.

revisionCard.summary: Coding–decoding = find the hidden shift. Compare one letter with its code to measure the shift, confirm on a second pair, then apply the same shift to encode or the OPPOSITE shift to decode. Use A=1…Z=26 for big shifts, and wrap around after Z.

gameMission.title: Secret Agent Cipher
gameMission.brief: Intercept the code, measure the shift from one letter, and decode the message! Watch the direction — decoding shifts the other way.

realLifeProject: Invent a +4 shift code and write a short secret message to a friend. Give them one letter's decode as a clue and see if they can crack the rest.

rememberIt.hook: One letter reveals the whole shift
rememberIt.unpack: Measure the shift from a known pair, apply it forward to encode or backward to decode.

studentQuestions.q: What if different letters seem to shift by different amounts?
studentQuestions.a: Then the rule isn't a simple shift — check for reversing the word, +1/+2 alternating, or position-based rules. Test your rule on every letter before trusting it.

studentQuestions.q: How do I handle a shift that runs past Z?
studentQuestions.a: Wrap around: after Z comes A. With positions, if the number goes above 26 subtract 26 (e.g. 27→1=A).
